utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we call the case, please, Madam Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution. I think that needs to be cleaned off, because otherwise we'll run the risk of a short circuit. I think in the meantime, while that's being done, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted by case manager Denise Gustin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I appear with Marela Jevtovic and Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau representing General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. I think one ought to advise the technicians in case they require to enter the room and --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour. The technician just informed me that we need to break for 20 minutes because we need to take the machine out. The water is going to damage the machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise there will be problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have done that before. And that's why I'm saying that we will probably need a break because I know what can happen. Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau, we'll resume in 20 minutes -- 20 minutes. Okay. In 20 minutes time. --- Break taken at 2.21 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. -- Sorry about that delay. Ms. Korner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are just a couple of administrative matters. The first is somewhat unfortunate. When there was an application by Mr. Cayley last week that the witness that was called by Mr. Nicholls should have protective measures, we were somewhat in haste and we said the next pseudonym up was BT22. That was from the protective measures we'd applied for. Regrettably what wasn't picked up by anybody was that there had been an earlier application by Ms. Sutherland, I think it was, to treat -- to call a witness BT22. So we went through the whole of that session on Friday -- whenever it was -- calling him Witness BT22 well, not calling him, but it's headed. So we've now got two BT22s. I don't think he was addressed as Witness BT22, but all we need I think is probably a correction to the transcript that he will now become BT23 and a notation to that effect on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That shouldn't be a big problem unless anyone else sees any major problem that I don't foresee. But the other witness that Ms. Sutherland applied to have BT22 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was called already --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise it wouldn't have mattered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think -- Madam Registrar. What can we do. I think it shouldn't present any major difficulties. There may be one instance or two, maybe, when I myself may have referred to him as BT22, but I don't -- not directly, but indirectly I may have. So one might need to go through the transcript to figure that out. In any case, we can just enter for the record that with reference to the last witness that gave evidence during the sitting of Friday, 31st of May, the Trial Chamber notes that the pseudonym applied to the same witness should be BT23 and not BT22, as inadvertently established earlier. Accordingly, all documents related to his evidence, including the transcript of the said sitting, where applicable, will be amended accordingly, so as to reflect what is stated above. And we'll leave it at that. And if you have difficulties, Defence and Prosecution, and you want us to do something else, we'll do it, because this is things that happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it should cause any difficulties. As I say, it's not one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Calling throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. Except that we have to take care with our secretaries to have that done as well, because our records show him as BT22 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then while we're on the subject of witnesses and pseudonyms, we today -- although it's a little earlier than the three weeks disclosed to the Defence -- BT21 and Your Honours -- we also supplied copies to Your Honours' legal officer so that Your Honours can see the statement, although I say it's an advance. The last matter is this: It was an error made by me when giving the List of Documents that this witness was going to look at, I said -- I'll just get my own list. Sorry. I said 781.4. In fact, it's 7 -- it's P785. But Your Honour, when we get to it, I'll put it up on the ELMO. It's one of the documents that Judge Draganovic looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't think it's desperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, finally just this: I think Your Honour said on Friday that we would be sitting just till 6.30. So do I take it that the breaks will be 15 minutes rather than 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, this was what I was coming to before we had the waterfall. In these matters, as I tried to explain to you last week, I try first to make sure that you have discussed it amongst yourselves, and secondly that none of the technical staff and the interpreters have reason to complain. I mean, that's -- that's my major concern, because ultimately half an hour here and half an hour there doesn't change much. But I'm sure that everyone would be happier to leave this place 6 -- half an hour earlier. It does matter. My suggestion to you was as follows, that we would start at 2.15 sharp and break at 3.45. That's the first session of an hour and 30 minutes. Then we will have a quarter of an hour break, resuming at 4.00. And that second session will be of a hour and 15 minutes, from 4.00 to 5.15. And then we will resume at 5.30 and finish at 6.30 with the understanding that if at any given time the Defence require longer breaks in order to consult with their clients, because that may vary from day-to-day, then obviously we will have to make adjustments accordingly, not necessarily meaning that we will finish at 7.00. We could still finish at 6.00. I think we will need to adjust the time schedule as we go along and even when necessary. But if these -- if this schedule that I am suggesting to you is convenient and agreeable to all of you - and that includes the staff on either side of the courtroom - then we can go along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, in the light of today, are we going to have just the one break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the second thing I was going to suggest for today. If it's agreeable to you, that instead of having two breaks today, we will have just one break of 20 minutes or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Twenty minutes I'm sure will -- I'm sorry. I haven't got my microphone on. 20 minutes will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And may I have feedback response from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And the technicians. Okay. Thank you. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, the witness I understand is in the witness waiting room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher. May I ask you how long you anticipate your direct examination of this witness to last, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to say. I'm going to on the basis, I think Your Honours have heard enough for the time being about the build-up of the political events. I'm not going to go through much detail of that. It will certainly take all of today and possibly something of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He knows he's going to be here for a couple of days, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures in place here. Mr. Stojic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Wrong witness, Your Honour. This is Dr. Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. Because they put 7.76 in front of me. Yes. Dr. Sabanovic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've come here to give evidence before this Tribunal. And before you do so, according to our rules, you are required to enter a declaration -- to make a declaration that you will tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It's a kind of oath that you take, undertaking to tell us the truth. The statement that you are asked to make is on a piece of paper that you have in front of you. And I kindly ask you to read it out loud. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, just very quickly, sir, I will explain to you the -- what's going to happen. First of all, I'm the Presiding Judge, and I'm flanked by the other two Judges composing this Trial Chamber; Judge Agius from Malta, Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and Judge Taya from Japan. You will first be asked a series of questions by the Prosecutor, who today is represented by senior counsel Ms. Joanna Korner. And the Prosecution team is immediately to your right. To your left in the front row you have four persons. The three that are nearest to you represent the Defence team for Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, who stands accused here; while the lady at the extreme right of the front row is counsel for General Momir Talic, who also stands accused here. The three persons you see right in front of you are the members of the registry. The rest is legal staff. The procedure is you will first be asked -- be examined directly by the Prosecution, and that examination is expected to last at least today for sure and maybe some part of tomorrow. After that, you will be cross-examined by the two Defence teams. And when that's finished, you will be able to go home. Thank you. The important thing is that you try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. We don't want long stories. We want the truth. But please stick -- you are a professional man. Stick to the question that is put to you either from the Prosecution or the Defence. Don't try to go off at a tangent or give us explanations that we don't need or you haven't been asked to give. Ms. Korner, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, could you give us your name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you give us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Enis Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think if you pull your chair in a little, you'll find it easier. I think you're sitting a bit far away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 24th of June, 1942?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you by religion -- are you by religion a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's right, Dr. Sabanovic, that you have specialised as a cardiologist since 1984.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Until that year. Between 1980 and 1984.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm so sorry. You're quite right. Having qualified from -- or graduated from medical school in 1968.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you said, you specialised in cardiology for four years. And having completed your specialisation did you move to the medical centre in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I worked there before. I had already worked in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact become the chief of that clinic or another clinic in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sanski Most. The internal medicine ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time of the outbreak of conflict in 1992, what position did you hold in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: In the health centre Sanski Most, there is a detached department of the hospital in Prijedor. And I was head of this internal medicine department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again at the time of the outbreak of the conflict in 1992, were you married?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of what ethnicity is your wife?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: She's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have children?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Three sons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Sanski Most, whereabouts did you live? I'm going to ask you, actually, if you could look at a map which has been marked P757.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going ask that it be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so if you could indicate to the Trial Chamber the area roughly in which you lived.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Right here, in the centre of the town on the left bank of the Sana, near the municipal hall of Sanski Most, because across the river is the municipal hall of Sanski Most, which is on the right bank, and I am on the left bank right next to the Sava, in the centre of the town, Omladinska Street BB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was that area inhabited by Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, or was it a -- was there one particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Multi. It was multi-ethnic, Muslims and Serbs and Catholics, and there were even some Romany not far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can take the map away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in 1990 become a member of the executive board for the SDA party in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But -- yes. I'm sorry. And as a member of the executive board, did you also attend meetings of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was a councilman in the municipal assembly, the Assembly of the Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the events that took place in 1991 when the war with Croatia started. Was there then a -- an order for the -- for men to report to the army, mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 99 per cent were summoned to Jasenovac which was the border between Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in the issuing of medical certificates for military-aged men who did not respond to the draft?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For them and actually to everybody who asked me for it. I was a physician. And as the head of the internal medicine service, I issued certificates regarding somebody's fitness -- rather, somebody's mobilisation, whether people could go to war or not. And I believe that I kept back some 1800 to maybe 2.000 people. I helped them not go to war because I did not think that one should go to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, are you saying that some of the people to whom you issued medical certificates, in fact were fit to go?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were those who were able-bodied. And let me also tell you. There were equally Serbs and Croats and Muslims amongst them. There were even Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that your belief was these people shouldn't have to go to war.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. I was not under obligation, and I didn't go to any war. I did not think it was time to wage war. I did not think that war was a way leading to the solution of problems, be it between states or municipalities or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of the medical certificates you had issued, were you visited by two officers from the military court in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It didn't happen only once. It happened two or three times. They were not officials. They were officers in the Yugoslav People's Army. One was a major, and another one was Captain First Class. The first time I think came two and on another occasion I believe came three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they want to verify the validity of these medical certificates?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did want to verify it, but truth to tell I disagreed with that, because they were not the ones. That is, people who were waiting in front of the surgery, they fled when those officers turned up. And I told them that I was in the right, that those were people who should not go to war, who should work, that Bosnia was an underdeveloped country, or rather, a country where there was no reason for war or go to war, so that they left -- they greeted me politely and left. But they were there on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually -- well, did they tell you that you had no right to issue the medical certificates?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They did not say I did not have a right to issue those certificates. They simply said that they would examine it all and that it wouldn't be all right if too many men were relieved of the war, that is, of the army duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal very briefly, if I may, with the events that led to the takeover in Sanski Most. Did the 6th Krajina Brigade take up residence in the area of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of March, 1992 -- on the 15th or 16th. I am not quite sure about that. Simply, I didn't give it much thought. But it was the 15th or 16th or perhaps the 17th of March -- the 6th Krajina Brigade, led by Colonel Basara. I was at a meeting with him two or three times. That is how I know his name. And it was deployed. In it there were no Muslims nor Croats nor Romany. It was solely composed of Serbs. And they came from Lusci -- they went to Lusci Palanka, Sanski Most about 30 kilometres from Sanski Most. And then they were brought to a hill near Sanski Most, quite near it they had heavy weaponry, several officers with them, and yes, their leader was Colonel Basara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were various checkpoints set up by the army and police around Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. After that, at that time when the 6th Krajina came, there were none. But after that, various checkpoints were set up, and it is quite a fact. I am sorry I have to say that. But they were set up by the Serbs to keep Muslims and Croats under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the non-Serb population, that is, mainly the Catholic or Croat and the Muslim, also set up their own patrols or barricades around the areas that they occupied?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were such places too. I did not take part in this because I was in the town and I was kept very busy because there were very many sick people. But yes, Muslims and Catholics together set up their guards in their villages to guard their homes at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you were told that you could no longer go on working?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who came to tell you that you could no longer go on working?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Before that, I was sort of a chief. But one morning, on the 25th or the 26th of April, 1992, Mladen Lukic and two or three more members of the Serb Democratic Party came and other fellow physicians came who were Serbs. There was a young intern, Bosko Grubisa and Ljilja Kasagic who was the director of the health centre and some others. I don't really remember them all. And I was literally told then that the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most was relieving me of my office as the director of the specialist service. Ljilja Kasagic is a Serb and she was also removed two days later. And a new physiologist was appointed the director of the health centre. His name was Milutin Dilas. And this young intern, Bosko, he was a member of the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most. He wore a uniform. He was a reserve captain. And he was in a uniform then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look, please, at a document, P624, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And perhaps we can put the English version up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could look at P624 B, the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'd like the witness to have the B/C/S version and the English version on the ELMO. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look, please, at paragraph 8 of that document. If understood --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, if you could just move up the document slightly on the ELMO. You need to move it up the screen to get -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a Crisis Staff decision dated the 24th of April, 1992. And in paragraph 8, it says: "Mladen Lukic, Vinko, and Boro are tasked with preparing the appointment of the acting director of the health centre in Sanski Most. This decision is to be issued on Monday morning, i.e. on the 27th of April, 1992." And that -- Vinko and Boro appears Boro Savanovic. And I'm not sure at the moment who Vinko is.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: A long surname. Boro has a very long surname. I can't remember what it is. I knew it, but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, don't worry. I think we can see that. Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can see it. Savanovic, yes. That's right. Savanovic. Born in the village of Kozica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that -- are these the people you've told us that Milan Lukic was one of the people who dealt with -- who came to the hospital. Does this refer to what you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: All three of them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they also replaced, did they, a Serb who was the head of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why she was replaced?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because I would not allow to use -- to take the spare parts that belonged to the civil defence, to take all this to Jasenovac. And he [As interpreted] agreed not to send all of these reserve equipment to Jasenovac and that is why they replaced her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I see. She's she wasn't prepared to send the equipment up to Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record -- I mean, it's a minor thing. But the previous -- the witness's reply is -- a person is referred to as a he and a her. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think he already told us it was a she.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But just for the record. I know that, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ljilja Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you may proceed, Ms. Korner. Sorry about that. But just for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you given an explanation why you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Why? That was evident. Yes, it was explained. Because I was a Muslim, because I was a head there. That is the reason, one sentence. No need for much talk here. They started it, selection, a genocide of Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It already started earlier in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And at that time the turn of Sanski Most came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give you any sort of written document, or was this just a verbal dismissal?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No document. Only verbally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after they told you that you were going to have to leave, did you actually continue working any longer at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I stayed on for a few days more. And after that, they would not allow me to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the 26th, 27th of April, you no longer worked at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see -- I'm going to move on now. So we can take the document away. Thank you. Did you see the attack on the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. Because there was only the Sana River between us, between my house and the municipal hall, because we face each other. I am on the left bank about 10 or 15 metres away from the bank, and the municipal hall -- right across the Sava there is the Sanus Hotel and then the municipal hall of Sanski Most. Right across the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see who was doing the attacking?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for me to look. One knew that. I was not there. They were -- the defence were part of the Muslims and Croats, the SDS which had already taken Sanski Most SUP and the power. First they issued an ultimatum to abandon the municipal hall and then they attacked it. And that is the truth. I saw it from my house. It was in late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to know who was doing the attacking. The military?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Why the military. They were all the military. They were all military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The domicile population and those who came with the 6th Krajina Brigade, as the army, as -- the Yugoslav People's Army. The 6th Krajinas. But the Serbs were all mobilised, so that they were military, yes, wearing camouflage uniforms. Oh, yes, and the police too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to the time of your actual arrest. But before I do that, did you own a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't have one now. I didn't have it before. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your arrest, did you hear announcements on the radio that anybody with weapons should surrender them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move to the day of your arrest. Were you arrested on the 26th of May of 1992 whilst you were at home?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, perhaps I can explain briefly. When I read the records, or rather, the statements, there were some dilemma assessed to them namely, I was arrested from home. But my colleague Bosko Grubisa called me around 8.00, that there was a very severe patient and that I should go there because he needed to consult me. And I went there by car, and we examined that patient together, and he told me that the road Banja Luka-Prijedor was Savo Tubje's [phoen] and we agreed about the patient. And as we came out, we saw policemen in front of it. There were two policemen who said that they would see me home. My home is about 400 metres away from the hospital. And I said, "Well, why? Why should you?" And we came out and -- yes. There were two more policemen in -- in the car, in their vehicle, a Campanola. But we went to my home and they told me to go in and to put some sports clothes on because they would be taking me for an interview to the police station in Sanski Most. So that I was arrested and I wonder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I wonder why was I called then because the situation was not all that bad. And where did these policemen right in front of the health centre at the time when I was invited to go there. My colleague was a member of the Crisis Staff. So I came out of the house after I'd put on some sports clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment I'm going to come to the actual arrest?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Yes, please do go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that you had gone to the hospital because you'd been asked to examine a patient, and then some policemen escorted you home and there was some other policemen there.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: All four came together by car from the hospital to my house together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you'd got to your house, is that when you say they told you that you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. At the time they told me to go inside, to change into sports clothes. Only one of them got out of the van. And told me to come back because they would be taking me to the Crisis Staff for an informative interview. I did so, and as soon as I entered the vehicle I realised what was happening, because I started to be mistreated. And I reached SUP under the feet of these four policemen, under their feet I was. And they had these rifles of this size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you got into the car, they made you lie on the floor; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: They pushed me down. There was like a bench in the van, and they threw me down and started trampling on me with their feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you were then taken to the SUP. Where were you placed when you got to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, there was no interrogation. They took me to the toilet and locked me in there, and I spent just under two days there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any of your papers with you, your identification papers?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It was burnt. They were burnt before I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you left what? Your home?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police entered the house. All this was rigged. And they took what they wanted. I think it -- my story would be too long if I were to tell you all the things they took from the house, my documents, my student's booklet, my ID card and everything was burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, doctor, if you leave it to us we'll tell you and the Judges will tell you when you're getting too long. Are you -- are you saying that at the house before you were put into the van, the police entered your house?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they searched it.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't really search a lot. They were looking for my documents, and they took them. They took my student's booklet, my ID card, my driving licence, and I don't remember the rest. They did ask me about weapons. They didn't find any, nor could they take any because they didn't find any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you told us that once you arrived at the SUP, you were kept there in a toilet for two days. Were you given any food?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how big was this toilet?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly 2 metres -- no, less. 2 by 2, something like that. I'm unable to tell you exactly. I think less than 2 metres by 2. It was a square room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any -- was there a window or ventilation?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so presumably all you had to sit on was the actual toilet itself.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot to mention, I had handcuffs on my hands. I forgot to mention this. However, in Bosnia it's like a field toilet. It doesn't have a proper toilet to sit on. After a day and a half or two, the police appeared in the evening, about 8.00 or 9.00, and they took me out of that toilet. So it was between one and a half days and two that I spent there. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to look for a moment, please, at Exhibit -- no, I'm sorry. It's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you look, please, at Exhibit P668. And it's the second -- it's the document -- the second page of the document headed "List of the most radical extremists."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't even need to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you looked at it before, but if we could put again --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless. Number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'd just look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Could we look at the other, please. It's the English headed "List of the most radical extremists." It's the second page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you've already identified, doctor, are you shown as number 4 on that list?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were described as a most radical extremist?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it's not clear to me to this day and never will be. I would bring the whole general staff to Sanski Most of the former Yugoslavia, headed by Petar Gracanin and another 15 generals and the commander of the Banja Luka Corps, and they came to Ostra Luka together with the president of the Sanski Most municipality, and I knew everyone from General Daljevic, who was party secretary attached to the general staff of Yugoslavia. He comes from the same village as I do. I knew several other national heroes, generals that I treated. And once Djurin Predojevic, a national hero from the First World War fell ill staying at his sister's and he fainted in the toilet. I participated and asked for a helicopter from Zagreb to be brought there. They didn't send it, and then we had him sent to Banja Luka and from there to Zagreb to a hospital there. Also, there's a village about 20 kilometres from Sanski Most, and General Daljevic's parents were living there Jelasinovci and Grdanovci and Lusci Palanka, a large number of generals from the Second World War came from those parts, and I was on good terms with all of them. I was a member of the party, of the League of Communists, when I was appointed as head of the health centre. Anyway, most of the Serbs have gone back to Sanski Most. They come to see me even now. I got a plaque from the Serbian civil council saying that -- expressing gratitude to the health centre, saying that there was no distinction by colour, by religion, and so on. So simply I will never understand why. I don't know. Probably because they had this ideology of genocide, annihilation, the creation of a new state without Muslims or Croats. That's a fact; no one can deny it. The director who stage managed all this is here. That is the only reason. There can be no other. I never hurt anyone. Even this summer I was in Banja Luka, for instance, and Dr. Milanovic was vice-president of the Serbian republic, from the very beginning when it was formed. Three months ago I exchanged greetings with him in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he's finished. I know what Mr. Ackerman -- he's not answering the question. But I think he has, in fact, answered the question, Your Honour. It's a long answer, but it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's -- obviously it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously it's an area about which the witness is very sensitive, especially -- I think we have covered it. Do I read you well, Mr. Ackerman? You may proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about one thing you've just said. You said, Dr. -- You said the director who stage managed all this is here. You were talking about the idea of the creation of a Serbian state. Who do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Milosevic, because Milosevic was the president of Serbia, the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the commander of the armed forces and everyone knows how the ideology started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've answered the question. Thank you very much, doctor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can take the document away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you were explaining that you were kept in this toilet without food or water for two days. What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The police came -- I assume it's the police. I don't know. I can't even say, because they had a white ribbon here, and it said "the Serbian youth" on it. Four or five of these young guys appeared, and they took me to Betonirka which is about 100 metres from Sanski Most to SUP downhill, to a garage there. This used to be a company for the construction of concrete tubes, and I was shut up in this garage. I had been beaten already, so they didn't feel these beatings I got. I couldn't look through -- I couldn't look at all. My eyes were swollen. I looked like a pig, I must say, with apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said that you had been beaten already. When were you actually beaten for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: In the vehicle, in the police vehicle that took me from the house to the SUP of the Crisis Staff, to the toilet there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And so you -- what, you said that you were under their feet. Were they doing something with their feet at that stage in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But they were wearing boots with rubber soles that do not cause such bruises as the blows in my head with fists and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people who took you from the toilet to Betonirka, did they do anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the people who hit me so badly that I looked awful. I couldn't see on either of my eyes because of the swellings, and my head was swollen and bruised all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they using to beat you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: They mostly used their fists, straight into the head. I had no injuries on my body from them; only my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything while they were hitting you with their fists?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, to tell you the truth, what they said and what they didn't say. If I were to recount it all, it would take a long time. They swore at me and so on. All kinds of words were used by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once you were taken to Betonirka, where were you put?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: There were several more people there; I can't tell you how many, but about 10 to 15 were there. And I sat down there in Betonirka, and that's how it started. They would come in the evening. They would call me out, take me outside and beat me. I must admit there was a policeman that I knew from before the war who was a guard, and he wouldn't let them. And I must admit that. The truth is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one of the policemen stopped other people beating you.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: For several nights. And the camp commander -- or rather the commander of this prison Miladin Papic who used to be police commander and I treated his family. He once resigned his position when he saw me and what I looked like. If it hadn't been for him, I -- I would have been destroyed there. I wouldn't have reached Manjaca. The beating I got, I got in Sanski Most, before getting to Manjaca. So there are people I need to thank and remember with gratitude for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beatings that you got in Manjaca -- I'm sorry, in the Betonirka, how often -- I'm sorry. I'll start the question again. How long were you kept there for in Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we were there until the 3rd, the 3rd, somewhere around there. I'm bound to make mistakes with dates. I didn't really study properly for this. It's not like as if I was sitting for an exam. I apologise for the joke. But while we were there, there were beatings. And also I went on a hunger strike, I want to tell you, for all of five days. In the toilet I didn't eat anything, nor did anyone offer anything. Afterwards they did offer food and water, but I wouldn't take any either. For five days I didn't eat or drink. I saw that that wasn't a good idea, and then I started taking water and so on, because maybe my assessment wasn't a good one. I was indifferent as to whether I lived or died, so I went on like that for five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that when you got there you think there were about ten people there. Were other people brought in?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw 10 or 15 people there when I arrived, but afterwards there were up to 50. There was no sitting. We had to stand. There was a small window about 30 by 30 centimetres in size - not bigger than that - there was no air. We were shut up. We had to stand up for days. There was no sitting room, not to mention room to lie down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody explain to you whilst you were there why you and the other people were being treated like this?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. It was common knowledge what the policy was and why this was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you've told us that you knew the commander of the police called -- Mr. Papric, I think.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander, that's right. The commander of the prison, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he never explain to you what was -- why this was being done to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't explain either, ever. But he did help me. Otherwise I would have been killed 100 per cent. I must repeat that he resigned at one point at the beginning when he saw what I looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you think you were in there for about three days or so. Were you then --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then transferred to a place called Hasan Kikic?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the Hasan Kikic hall in Klucka Street in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just have the map of the photographs back for a moment, that is, 757.1. If you'd just look at the photographs. Number 1 -- and can I tell you the photographs were taken last year, doctor. That's described as Betonirka. Is that what it looked like in 1992? I think you'd better have -- we don't need it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you'd just give it to the witness so he can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at photograph number 3, it has the legend HK school. But is that what the Hasan Kikic school looked like in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, yes. Just like that. That's what it looks like now. And behind is the sports hall belonging to that school, behind this part that is shown on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how many people were taken to the sports hall with you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me see. There must have been about 300 to 400 people, because there was a large number of garages, not just one there. Something like that. Afterwards the number increased, so that two days later one night, about 1.00 a.m., about 200 men were brought in by trucks from Kljuc. So we were packed full. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the sports hall, were there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can get rid of the map now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the sports hall, were there any beds?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean beds? There wasn't room. There were more than 500 people in that gym. And if you lie down, you have to lie against the wall. So there were no beds. We didn't need beds. If only they had spared us the beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened if you needed to use a toilet?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a policeman would escort men. Those of us who were there, we didn't go to the toilet often. We didn't eat much. We were fed rarely. So a policeman would escort people out, and people often didn't want to go. They didn't dare to go to the toilet because they would be beaten on the way there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were guarding you there, were they ordinary policemen or military policemen?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a war. There are no ordinary policemen any more. There's a war on. It's all over. And this is the police. They were all policemen. Now, whether they were military or the other, I don't know. But anyway, they were the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of uniforms were they wearing? Were they wearing the blue uniforms worn by the police, or were they wearing camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: There were of both kinds, camouflage and those worn by the former police force that was known at the milicja before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that people wanted to go to the toilet they were beaten. Did other beatings take place? During the night, during the day, or both?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. This is such a broad question. Every moment, all the time there was beating, especially during the night. It was constant. People were lying in a coma. Three or four men were unconscious. I can't understand that these people survived. To do something like this and not have them treated in neurosurgery, I just can't understand that a man can survive such things. There were -- the treatment we got was such that it cannot be recounted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a doctor. Were you allowed to give any sort of medical treatment to any of these people?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: In that gymnasium, next to me about 4 metres away there were four or five men in a coma, unconscious. I couldn't, though I was looking at them, facing them -- I was not allowed to get up and examine them, never mind give them any kind of treatment. No one wanted anyone to be treated. They wanted people to die.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody who was near you who had, instead of neurological injuries, had any sort of other injuries that you could see?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, right close to me was a Catholic who had been wounded in a village near Sanski Most, and there was shelling from a hill called Magarice by the 6th Krajina Brigade. And the shell hit him here. He had an open wound. I didn't think he would survive because he was never bandaged. He would be taken for dressing, and he would be brought back beaten up. And those who treated him was a dentist. There was so many proper physicians, GPs and specialists, but Davidovic, who was a dentist, treated them, and he would allow people in this condition to be beaten, beaten to death, without even treating their wounds, which is why they came to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just pause for a moment you indicated when you were describing this man's wound -- and I just want you to confirm this is right, because we need a note of it -- you indicated the right, as it were, top of the thigh. Was that where his injury was?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was a wound there, a penetrating wound from a shell or a piece of shell, a shrapnel it was festering and infected. But none of this counted, so that no aid was given to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described there was a dentist called Davidovic. Was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was -- he was the person who was treating people, so-called?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the medical platoon or team or people who were supposed to treat and extend first aid when someone asked for aid, if he dared ask for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, what about food? Was food brought? I think you said it was.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did bring food to that sports hall; very little of it. Sometimes they would -- some Serbs would come and bring food from family members. This was rare, but there was an organised system too. In the morning, they would bring these large containers with cups. But how can you when people had to relieve themselves in there? It was dreadful. The sunlight would come in through the big windows, and you were living inside in a stench that one can't stand. People were urinating and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any facilities to wash or to clean up in any way?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Nobody even asked for that, because there was no time for any washing. I must tell you that I spent more than two and a half months without a bath, and I still am not suffering from any skin disease or anything. Nobody asked for it because nobody dared to. You -- all you care about is how to survive, not to get anything. So people were too afraid to ask for something, even if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to come to the last night that you were kept at the sports hall. What happened to you that night?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That night -- that evening, sometime between 7.00 and 8.00, a man -- a short man with a long stick wearing clothes like the pilots wore before the war or some policemen came with this long wooden stick and asked me to come out to the place to where in the kitchen the food was prepared. He told me to come out with him and told me that that night he was the boss, that he was the commander, and that commander, whose name was Martic from the village near my village -- I don't know whom he -- what he did to others, but he treated me decently. His village is some 15 kilometres from mine; that is, from Sanski Most. And of course I examined his mother and of course I examined her before the others so that she could catch the bus to another village -- so that he treated me decently. Otherwise whenever he entered this sports hall, everybody had to stand up, put one's heads down and stand. And then further according to the orders. But however, he left me alone. He never laid a finger on me. But that night he did not come and he is the boss -- or rather, he is the head of this sports hall. Instead this short man. And I heard that his name was Rajlic and took me out, and three more young men came with rifles and they kept cocking and uncocking their rifles, and they made me go down on my knees and to mop the floor with a rag. And I did that for more than two hours. And I still can't stand -- I cannot stand up because my spine hurts. I simply cannot understand certain things in medicine, diseases, the mistreating -- I mean, all sorts of mistreatment that one survives. And yet a minor thing and you can never recover. So there was this beating and then they said that I'd be going either to Manjaca or something called Srbrenestijele [phoen], near Knin, that never -- that I'd never treat anyone, that they'd pull my nails. And that night I wanted to hang myself. I wanted to hang myself. And there was this large window in the sports hall with metal locks or handles, and I got two shirts which I was about to tear to hang myself with. But nevertheless my conscience all of a sudden started waking up and I -- I thought what my -- Enis would say, you didn't -- Serbs killed you. You didn't kill yourself. And I thought about that, that I shouldn't kill myself. And I gave it up. But it was a very bad night. The next day when we left off to Manjaca -- and there was then -- there were then those questions of where's Sabanovic and there was again beating in front of the trucks and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you one more question. You told us that you were forced to mop the floor. And then you told us about your spine. As well as mopping the floor, were they doing anything else to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, rifle butts here in the neck area and spine, and mistreatment and beating, beating, kicking and fists. And that was the worst night for me, and that is why I wanted to hang myself. But thinking about the future, the history, and I thought well, my children will say it wasn't the Serbs who killed my -- our father but he killed himself. And then I decided not to kill myself, to let them do it. And somehow I felt better after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me, doctor, this seems a silly question. But had anything -- had you ever received treatment like you received in those days in the sports hall and Betonirka -- had anything like that ever happened to you before?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Before? Well, it couldn't -- nothing like that could happen like that, because I never had any trouble with him. I was never ill, but -- and whilst I was in the WC -- no, nobody ever -- nobody ever came to see me let alone offer some help. No, out of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my fault. Had you ever been subjected to this sort of humiliation and attack by anyone before?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I was held in high regard. Dignity. I lived with dignity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us it was the next day that you were taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the first lot of prisoners to go to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first lot, the first group of 147 [Realtime transcript read in error "villages"] individuals in three trucks. From another hall and from this one. But some were allowed to leave. Not all of them went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to for a moment to look, please, at one document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there is a mis -- an error. I believe that there is an error in the transcript. 147 villages. I do not think that was what he said. I believe he said 147 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. In the transcript it says 147 villages in three trucks. Just for the record --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Individuals, people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hadn't looked at the ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just look --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at document P666.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we'll just put the English up on the ELMO. Your Honour, it's not on the list. It's just to confirm the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have 667 but not 666.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not 666. That's the one before. If you'll just put the English on the ELMO, you'll see ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order to the public security station to evacuate 150 prisoners to Manjaca, dated the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Has the witness got it? Oh, it's on the back, I see -- the B/C/S. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can just confirm it.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're telling us that you -- there were 147 people -- it may not. The difference of three, don't worry about -- who went with you that day to Manjaca. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. This is the truth, 147.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We don't need the document any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you accept that it was on or about the 6th of June of 1992 that you went to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Of course I didn't know the date when I left. There was no way I could note the dates. So as of the WC onward, I simply don't know anything about that. I didn't have anything, nor -- nobody explained it. Nobody mentioned it. Nobody cared what date it was. But yes, it must have been there give or take.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say there were 147 people. How do you know the number that was taken with you to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing. When we from the sports hall left in a truck to SUP, from another hall from the town two more trucks arrived, and we went to Manjaca. We didn't know. We thought they were taking us for an exchange. But then we reached a village, and then when they took us over a very high mountain then we reached Manjaca. Perhaps we'll have to go back again. But when we fetched up in Manjaca -- when we got to the hall, in the cow shed, the pavilion, whatever they called it -- that evening -- that is how I know it -- a policeman and I went and somehow in Manjaca my impression was that I was somehow in a more favourable position. And that policeman and I went and counted those men. And they were lying down with their head like this and legs like this. And this was a long cow shed, 60 to 70 metres. And we counted 140. And he told me that 147 had been brought to Manjaca -- had arrived in Manjaca, which means that seven men, seven individuals, had disappeared. And that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned something that happened the next morning. Before you got on the trucks that took you to Manjaca, was anything else done to you or any of the other men?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. It was horrible, because there was particularly bad beating as one entered those trucks. So I somehow tried to jump up like a dog. I leapt into that truck. Then it was very hot. And in front of the SUP they were putting -- they were throwing -- they were making more people get into these trucks. They were tied with something. Their hands were tied two by two, so that it was -- the whole thing was horrible. But nevertheless they all reached Manjaca safe and sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of -- did all the men come from the sports hall, or did some of the men come from another place in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from other places too, I think, but I can't really know that. I know from the sports hall in the town, some of them, and we from this Hasan Kikic sports hall. But yes, there were people from villages around and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Manjaca, who met you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The police met us. The police which was to run Manjaca, which was the run the camp the few -- the administration of the future camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. By "police" do you mean military police or ordinary policemen like those who worked in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the military place. And I was told when we got off the trucks, we again had to stand by those trucks with our arms up. And they beat us again. But somehow he skipped me during that beating. That policeman who beat everybody, he somehow did not beat me. And I just looked a little bit -- because you were not supposed to turn around. But I saw a dark shortish man in a uniform, and he had the rank of lieutenant in the Yugoslav People's Army, and he told the policeman, "This is a doctor for you," and pointed his finger at me. I could see him. But those policemen -- that is, one just said, "Well, not even the international Geneva Convention will help him here." And that's how it started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could we take this a little more slowly, please. You say there was a JNA lieutenant there.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told the other policemen that you're a doctor. Do you know how he knew you were a doctor?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it will take too long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt that he was the -- that he was a son of a teacher in the teacher's academy in Banja Luka. And for a while I worked in Banja Luka at a clinic there. And I had a patient who was a teacher, a tall man. He had a heart complaint. And when I turned, I saw that he was that teacher's son who used to visit his father, and he was in the ward where I used to work. And that is how I knew that I was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's how he knew that you were a doctor. The translation came across --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That is how he knew, yes. He recognised me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this JNA lieutenant seem to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: We were told that he would be the head, that he would be the warden of the camp. That is what we were told as we were standing by those trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to jump ahead a moment, we know that somebody called Lieutenant Colonel Popovic took over the camp. How long after this did he take over?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: A few days later -- Popovic did not take over from him, because there is a camp warden and a camp commander. Popovic was the commander of the camp, and he had his wardens. And this lieutenant left three or four days later. He took up some other duty, and he never again showed his face in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this lieutenant who was the warden of the camp, did he explain to you how you should behave in the camp? For example, how you should talk to guards.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. We were explained that the next morning by a sergeant of the Yugoslav army in -- or a corporal. And he was wearing an SMB uniform. It was rainy so the grass was wet as we were taken to the cow shed. And we were taken to this first cow shed. And he told us to keep quiet, not to move about, because there is no court here. This is a camp. If you -- so you either -- you have to stand, to stand like this, and you behave as if you were to -- hands at your back, head down, regardless of conversation, regardless of where you are. You have no right to move. If the worms are moving under your feet, then they are there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like a translation of that last -- well, perhaps I better ask again. You said something about worms under your feet. Who said what, using that expression?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I think it's better if you just tell us again what was said to you about -- and particularly how the expression --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: What was said was -- well, that expression was or you trample a worm or you kill a man. There is no court in the camp. And he told us how to behave or how we were -- what posture we were to take when talking to an official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to go back to this. Who was saying and how were they saying it, you trample a worm or you kill a man. There is no court in the camp. What exactly was being said? That's what I'm trying to get at?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. That was the sergeant who was standing there. The door is very large, is very wide, and he stood there and warned us to avoid any trouble, to obey, to just heed to orders as they came from superiors. And he was a sergeant in the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army. There at Manjaca was a training centre, that is, where people used to do their military service before the war and so on and so forth, so that there was a young man there whom I never saw again, after where I -- because seven people were killed there. He was caught three days earlier before we left to Manjaca. He was caught in Sanski Most. And he said, "I'll be fine there, because that's where I did my military service. That is where they have the training ground for the artillery, for the army, that is where the army used to be. It is a very large ground and it is -- and the troops used to come in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: -- to that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to have one final attempt at trying to get this clear. The sergeant was addressing you. He was telling you how you had to stand when you spoke to the guards. He told you there was no court here -- in the camp, rather, and that --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Killing -- that there was -- killing a man and worms under your shoes or feet. Were what?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It was for comparison. Because there was some rain, and there were all those worms in the grass. And as he stood by this door, he said, "Well, you either squash a worm or kill a man, all the same. No difference. No court, no accountability."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough, Ms. Korner. And if it is convenient for you, we could stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For 20 minutes. We'll have a break at 20 minutes, resuming at quarter to 5.00. Quarter to 5.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you told us that when you'd been pointed out as a doctor, somebody had said that the international Geneva Conventions didn't apply to Manjaca. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to have a look at a document, please, that comes from the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't recall him saying exactly -- saying it exactly the way that you put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I was summarising, Your Honour. But I'm perfectly happy if anybody can actually find the actual quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What he said, I recall is that he said more or less that a remark was passed when it was pointed out that he was a doctor-- a remark was passed that the Geneva Conventions won't be of any help to him. But it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I'm sure Your Honour has got a much better memory than I have for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think we better --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. "Would help him here."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because they -- they would not be applied. And that is -- that the International Geneva Convention won't be of any help to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what he -- this is what he said, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. "Well, not even the International Geneva Convention will help him here."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's how it started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, at a document. It's the document they I handed in together with the proofing document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So perhaps that could be handed to the witness. And Your Honours, I'd ask that it be made Prosecutor's Exhibit 806. And I just want the witness to have the B/C/S version, please, which should be separate from the English version. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate, doctor, that you hadn't seen this until you looked at it on Saturday. But if we can just go through it, because I want to ask you about a couple of things in it. It's from the assistant commander for moral guidance, it looks like. But anyhow, it's to deliver to the warden of the Manjaca camp, personally inspect how prisoners of war are being treated. And it was -- originally it appears as an order sent to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps from the Main Staff, and talks about setting up proper accommodation for prisoners of war, setting up of prisoner of war camps. And then it says: "Respect the provisions of international laws of war in all treatment of prisoners of war. Put prisoners of war in prisoner of war camps as quickly as possible." And then so on and so forth. Now, what I want to look at is the next document which sent -- which comes from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps on the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The interpreters should have this document. They do have this -- I just heard the interpreter saying could we put it on the ELMO. It is actually attached to the document they were given earlier this afternoon. But however, if it's required to be put on the ELMO, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you're now referring, I assume, to the second of these documents. That is, the one which in the English version ends with the three numbers 892; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I can hear somebody saying through my headphones put it on the ELMO, so we will. Could that be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be 807, P807.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's all part of the same document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's all part of the same document, Your Honour. Yes. And I think can I perhaps take the B/C/S away from the witness. It's easier if I find it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
