utterances.text: Now, what I think we're looking at here is a document 13th of June, 1992. It's all handwritten -- from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. And it states that "The commanders of the prisoner of war camps in Stara Gradiska and Manjaca shall send daily reports on the arrival of prisoners of war to the assistant camps commander for moral guidance and legal affairs." And then it goes on about lists of prisoners who shall be exchanged. And then: "Enclosed, application of the provisions of international laws of war in the treatment of prisoners of war and civilians." And as it's all we can see that it was delivered to the chief -- the order was to be delivered to the chief of security of the 1st Krajina Corps, the commander of Stara Gradiska prisoner of war camp, and Manjaca and other various people. And now can we look at the enclosure, which is headed "Application of the provisions of international laws of war in the treatment of prisoners of war and civilians." I think you'll find, sir that, that's the next document you have underneath, if you turn to the next -- if you take that one away and I think you'll find that it's there. Now, I just want to look at some of the conventions that the commander of Manjaca was being reminded of. "Prisoners of war must be humanely treated at all times. Any unlawful act or omission by the detaining power causing death or seriously endangering the health of a prisoner of war in its custody is prohibited. No prisoner of war may be subjected to physical mutilation or experiments. Prisoners of war must be protected against all acts of violence or intimidation, insults, and public curiosity. Measures of reprisal against prisoners of war are prohibited and their persons and their honour must be respected in all circumstances." Doctor, in a moment I'm going to ask you about what happened in Manjaca. But from what you saw, were -- was any adherence to those conventions given -- was any adherence made to those provisions in Manjaca while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. Not a single one of those provisions, and I've known -- I knew them before. None of them were respected, were complied with, and they were very far from reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm just going to look at a couple more. "All prisoners of war shall be treated alike, without any discrimination on grounds of race, nationality, religious belief, political opinions, or any other similar criteria." Then it talks about particulars. "All forms of coercion or torture are prohibited," and so on and so forth. As far as you were concerned, doctor, were the majority of prisoners at Manjaca actually prisoners of war, in the sense that is meant by these conventions?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you quite sincerely and truthfully all those who came from Sanski Most, who came from Kljuc -- I don't know about others, because I wasn't in touch with them -- but the people from Sanski Most, there was no resistance in our town. There was no war. There wasn't a shot fired when we were captured in our homes or at our working places. So there was no war there at all. There was no resistance. I loved when the CNN would come and other international broadcasters and they would say, "This one was captured on the front." I can't understand this, and I deny it. I cannot talk about it at all, not a single one. I am very familiar with the municipality of Sanski Most. Not a single person, not a single detainee from Sanski Most at Manjaca was a prisoner of war. There was no war. There was no resistance. A couple of policemen would simply bring 50 people from a particular village. What kind -- what resistance, what front line, what war are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just look at a couple of other things that are talked about here. "Moneys and articles of value may be temporarily taken away from prisoner of war, only by order of the commander of the unit or camp and with an appropriate receipt." Now, when you and the other men arrived at the camp, did anybody have any valuables on them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't, but some people did. I told you that I counted the men with a policeman one by one, and then I saw another colleague of mine, a physician from Sanski Most. I didn't know that he had arrived at Manjaca. He came from a different sports hall. And as he was lying on his stomach with his head in the straw and his hands on his back, I didn't recognise him. But the police took his watch off. He had a nice watch on. And he turned around, and then I saw that it was my colleague, a specialist of occupational medicine, and that he had worked in Sanski Most. And I saw his watch being taken off myself. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what happened to other prisoners who had any valuables left.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that they were taken away, but I didn't see it I don't I can't tell you about things I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally this, because everybody can read the whole document themselves. It says that "In camps, prisoners of war have the right to elect representatives every 6 months by secret ballot. A representative must be a prisoner of war who has same nationality, et cetera. The representative represents the prisoner of war before the military authorities protecting power, international committee of the Red Cross, any other organisation that assists them. And prisoners, representatives are exempt from all other work." Was there any such election of a representative that took place whilst you were in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Never any attempt of that kind had been made. If it had been done, there would have been trouble. There was no election, no representatives, no opinions, nothing. You just had to do what you were ordered to do. If you didn't, you knew what lay ahead for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we come to this: "Civilians who have fallen into the power of a warring side are entitled to respect for their persons, honour, family rights, beliefs, and customs. These individuals must be treated humanely at all times and all forms of violence and intimidation are prohibited." You told us that most of the people that -- who were from Sanski Most and Kljuc were not prisoners of war. They were people who had been rounded up. Were you treated humanely, as the International Geneva Conventions say?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no humaneness or the slightest iota of the Geneva Conventions. There was violence, such as even Hitler never resorted to. I have read a lot about it and seen a lot, but what happened there only a well organised well-exercised campaign to destroy a people can achieve it. Nothing civilised happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can put the document away now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to that first day when you arrived. You've told us that you were seen there by a JNA lieutenant. And you've told us how you got out of the trucks. Was anybody injured or killed upon your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It came about as we were coming out of the truck -- trucks, jumping off, we were ordered to lean against the trucks with our hands up and our heads down. However, right next to me there was a grassy area. We were the first group to arrive. Right next to me there was a man, a young man, from Sanski Most, Merhardzic Neron, or something like that. He was killed right next to me straight away. He was killed. Also Biscevic, a dentist. I can't remember the name now. So as I was saying, 147 of us arrived there, but that evening around 7.00, 140 were counted in the stable. This was right in front of me. I watched with a rifle butt on the head, on the asphalt. People were killed by policemen from Sanski Most, not the police that was there when we arrived and that were in charge of the camp but policemen from Sanski Most. Out of those seven people that disappeared by the time we entered the stable, I told you that with the policemen we counted 140 -- but there was never any trace found of those seven missing people, nor their bodies, nor will they ever be found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you saw this man standing next to you being attacked with rifle butts. Did you see how the other people --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: He was thrown on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. The person next to you was thrown on the ground and then attacked with rifle butts; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Killed. Beaten and killed on the spot. We were standing there for half an hour, up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the deaths of the other six men or their bodies afterward?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see all of them. But the same that happened, it was said that those people had been killed. No one ever saw them again. But just as these two men right next to me were killed, I wasn't able to walk around. I wasn't a guard or a warden. I came here -- came there to be killed. And it was just by chance that I wasn't killed. That is the truth. Otherwise, the same would have happened as happened to this dentist and this young man who worked as a conductor. I saw these two being killed 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you were told about the others being killed. Who told you about them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It was said by the police. All kinds of rumours reached me. I had a little more freedom, especially that night. The bad reports about me hadn't yet reached them, so I expected it would be a kind of camp as envisaged by the Geneva Conventions. Unfortunately it was quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you've already told us that you were then taken to the stables and you were made to lie down and then a count took place.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: When we entered the stable, we lay down and I was called out. The others remained lying down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry. You've told us about that. When you arrived at Manjaca, was there a fence around the camp itself, or had that yet not been put up? A wire fence.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a fence. There were several men who came from the area of Doboj, four or five men, who were brought there from Stara Gradiska, and they were working on the fence. At first a mine had not been planted round the camp. Two or three days later, the camp was mined. I watched the mines being laid. Engineers of the army, of the Yugoslav army, the engineers laying mines. I watched them do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once the count had taken place in the stable, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: We had nowhere to go. They were in the middle of the stable. If you have the pictures, I'd show you. They stood there, five or six officers, then the policemen, a nurse wearing a uniform, and I was called to stand up, and they asked me questions: Would I like to go to Sanski Most to fight with them? I said I wouldn't go to fight against the people, only if I were a soldier with you and if somebody were to attack you I would defend you. And then they sort of baptised me, a policemen. I was standing up. I was the only one of all the detainees - and there were about 8.000 of them, though the number varied, but the maximum was 8.000 - so I was baptised then. A policeman came and told me that I had to learn by the next day how to cross myself. And I said I wouldn't do it and that was not possible. And then after that they called me -- I'm sorry. They asked me to join them, and we left the stable. We went outside. On both sides of me were two lieutenants wearing SMB uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. You're going a bit fast. The interpretation is lagging behind. Okay. You left -- there were two men in SMB uniform. And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I was between them. They were on either side of me. And I was moving and talking to them. They said, "We don't like this either, but we have to do it." Literally these were regular men military of the Yugoslav army. They said, "We'd like to go home too as soon as possible. We don't like this." And then we left the stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we move on to what you did then, two matters. First, when you said that you weren't prepared to be, as you put it, baptised, did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: You're wrong. Not -- I didn't say I wasn't ready. I was baptised on the spot, but I couldn't learn the 50 or 100 words that this man told me I had to learn. And I said that I wouldn't learn it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say you wouldn't learn it, did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The policeman hit me then in the stomach. I was skinny then, much thinner than I am now, and I dealt with it. He hit me with his leg. He kicked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you, please, a map with some photographs on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it's one we've produced yet. I don't think Your Honours have got it. The Defence have got it. So could that be handed to the witness and to Your Honours. And the exhibit number is 807, Exhibit 807.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were explaining about the stables. If you look at the photograph number 10, which says "Stable 1, inside view." Where were the people lying down? In front of the stalls?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the inside can be seen only on one photograph, the inside of the stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: They were lying with their head over there, like this, and their legs here. Then the next group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: They were in rows on the concrete. And this is where the livestock used to be tied. Everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll move on. We've got a bigger photograph somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you just -- I'll tell you what, doctor. If you just put the map on the ELMO. Somebody will come and do that for you. Oh, here we are. We've got a bigger one here. We've got the same one but bigger. If we can put that on the ELMO. And if you could just indicate, doctor, how people were lying.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: People were here on both sides. And two other rows in between, the length of this middle part, on the concrete. This is where the livestock used to be tied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: And a place where the livestock drank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were telling us that you were taken out of the stable with these two men who were telling you that they didn't want to be there. And were you then asked to examine some of the -- some people, some prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Not just the two of them but all of these who were in front. There were another four or five policemen in front and a nurse in uniform. Then they told me to examine four young men. I examined them. And the diagnosis was scabies, a skin disease that causes itching and provoked by dirt. It's called scabitox in Latin. And there were three or four young men. And a few days later, the police brought me -- I wrote down what was necessary. And the policeman brought four boxes of these kabatos [phoen], or rather, bottles of a medicine that you administered. And one young man had plaster on his arm up to his elbow, a cast. I was told to examine him. That was my assignment. And I found that that young man had a broken left shoulder and the cast went up to his elbow. You see, the cast is heavy. It's a load on the lower arm. And I have to be quite sincere. These officers and the management or the command of the camp gave me a referral note. I wrote it out. I filled it in. I don't have the tell you in Latin that he had a broken shoulder. A car came from Banja Luka and took him off to the surgical ward of the clinical centre in Banja Luka, and I don't know what happened to him after that. But I also --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: -- To tell you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. It -- Doctor, it's just -- it's my fault, but it's a bit confused. You're saying, first of all, that you were asked to examine four people who had scabies.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And shall we get that out of the way. Later did they provide something -- did the military provide some medicine for that? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And were those the -- were those men that you examined the people who had come from Doboj and were building the fence?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this man that you're now talking about, the man who went to Banja Luka hospital, you say that he had -- you examined him and he had a cast -- do you mean from his wrist to his elbow?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: From his elbow to the end of his hand. And I found a fracture in his left shoulder, which means that the cast made it worse. And he told me that he had been in Prijedor in the hospital there, that that is where they put on the cast, and then they sent him back to Sanski Most. He came there with us. He was the next one after the patients with scabies. And after I examined him, he was sent to Banja Luka. And I must add, I left immediately. In December I went to Switzerland. And afterwards this young man called me in Switzerland that he was alive and well and he thanked me very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So what you're saying is although he had a broken shoulder, the cast had been put onto his arm and that made his shoulder worse.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I can deal, please, with -- next with the food and water that first day. Were you given anything to eat or drink that first day of your arrival or that first night?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was thirsty and I was the first to get water to quench my thirst. And afterwards, together with the policemen, I went and distributed water to the people lying down. They were lying on their left elbow, and I gave them water to drink, to each and every one from the beginning to the end, and I was escorted by this policeman. There was no food on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did other prisoners arrive from other areas that same night -- or day?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not that night. I was something like the man on duty in the stable that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the following day? Did other people arrive?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: And then -- well, we'd have to spend two months here if I were to tell you everything. The number changed every day, and it went up. So the largest number was about 8.000-something. Otherwise, the numbers changed. New people came in and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry; did you say 8.000?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean in the whole camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I did. In the whole camp. More than 8.000. 8.000-something was the maximum number. 8.600 / 700. This was on one particular day. But the number kept changing every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you get these figures from?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in the clinic, and I had contact with the police and with the commander, and I knew of this. I was told. And anyway, you could see it. You've seen yourself a large settlement. And after July, in August and September there were people walking around between the stables, so things had settled down. And there were crowds of people walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that on that first night there were 140 of you in that stable. What was the maximum number of people that were kept in your one stable at any one time?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd say the stable that I was in, and the same would hold true of those others. In my stable, the largest number was 890 -- 890-something. And it was really very crowded and people moved out and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal now with Manjaca by way of topics. In other words, food, water, beatings, and killings, as I say, in topics. But first of all, can I ask you about this: You were a doctor, and you've told us that you saw another doctor that night in your stable. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Meho Derviskadic, who now lives in Switzerland. He did not want to testify because -- well, I don't know. He was admitted into Swiss nationality and so on and so forth. That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about whether he's going to testify or not. I just want to find out about the doctor-- the medical staff in the camp. There was you and Dr. Derviskadic. Was there also a male nurse named Asim Bajric?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other doctors in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on. But they didn't do the things that we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you and Dr. Derviskadic and the nurse Bajric, were you the only three who provided medical attention?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Right up until the arrival of inmates from Omarska, Keraterm and others from Prijedor. We were the only ones. And for the duration of my stay in Manjaca, we were the ones who took care of the inmates' health. Other doctors who arrived later on, they did take some part in distributing medicines around the stables locally and brought to the surgery to us -- they'd establish who were sick, and they would then bring them to our surgery. So they did not examine them. It was only the two of us -- the two of us doctors and that nurse. We were the only one who is did that, who treated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us where was your infirmary -- or clinic, first of all?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: In June -- so the first one was in the police building, in the building that the police was in. And later on about in the middle, nearer to these stables or pavilions as they called them. And then also in the camp command. Once upon a time it was the slaughterhouse, but that was refurbished and we had there a separate infirmary where we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you take the map and the photographs again. Have you still -- you've still got that. Yes. If we look at the photograph numbered "6" on that map.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Here. Mm-hm. I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see something called the admin building, administration building. Was that where your first clinic was?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Yes. It was right here, on this corner here, this longer side facing us and here in this part. And this here is where the police slept. But that is the administration building -- or the command. The administration building is when you run a company or something. But it's the command when it comes to the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then we can see -- and I just want you to confirm -- paragraph number 8, which is to the right-hand side as we look at it, is headed -- subtitled "Infirmary." Was that the building you used after that?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Infirmary." Is that it? The last one? You mean the last photograph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, photograph number 8.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: This here is not the infirmary. It is at the entrance in a small part in the front part. This is the entrance into stables where horses were kept. And we turned there into a hospital where we admitted severe cases and people who were bedridden and then we started sleeping also in that building. Before that, we slept in the stables with all the other inmates. But here we had -- well, at least 30 people severely afflicted who came to us frequently. And this here, behind this part, in the same building to the left you can see the door here. Facing us. That was the solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you -- you've lost me there slightly, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we put the thing on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think that's the way to go, because I'm getting confused --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Descriptions of doors and whatever don't help. If we could put the map on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you were indicating a door that you said was where the isolation cell was. Can you just point to that with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Here. This one here. And we entered through this other side. That is where we entered our hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: And this here on this side, it was the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but the door -- can you have the pointer again, please. The door that we can see with the little sort of roof over it, is that the entrance to the infirmary or hospital?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, it is not -- yes. On the front side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Somebody has moved the photograph out of the frame. All right. Point to where the entrance to the hospital was.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just there.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that door there. I see.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: This here. This small area here. This narrow door here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And when you say "isolation cell," was that an isolation cell for patients or for other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Isolation cells exist in armies. I did my service in Bjelovar before the war, 11 months something. But I was a doctor and I was in the infirmary. But an isolation cell is the area where you put unruly ones, unruly men in regular troops. And here they would put there those whom they saw as most dangerous and those who were beaten the worst, people who were taken out, away, and then put into this isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. We don't need the map any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to split the period. I'm going to ask you about medicines and the like. Before the arrival of the International Red Cross in July of 1992, what medicines did you have for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: None. No medicines at all. If something gets there, if an officer perhaps brings it along visiting, or if a visitor comes. We had no medicines, except what I just said about those four men, that is, those four inmates. We were given medicine for the scabies. Apart from that, there were no medicines. And perhaps today I could develop a modern thesis on health and human personality, what a man can go through unscathed without spending any medicines. Gentlemen, you are here -- I won't say they are much cleverer than I am. I know they are more experienced. I don't know if they are cleverer. But you are all intellectuals. A man who's on insulin, who suffers from diabetes, and he cannot live without insulin, he needs substitution for his pancreas, he needs something so as to live, so as to stop the sugar. We had such people there who were administered insulin in Prijedor around, and they were those saying they would not survive because there was no insulin and there were no tablets even. There were also drug addicts from Sanski Most, a young man who was on to drugs and he came with an eupyrene [phoen], that is, with some sedatives. He gets a pill for three or four days and he completely got rid of his addiction. And all those who were on insulin before, they all survived. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite all right. What sort of treatment were you able to give then to people who came to your clinic?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Examined them, gave them some massage, if they would have high fevers we would massage them with alcohol. That is what they gave us, alcohol and then we would massage them. And there were people who were wounded. We also had some wounded. And there were also those who came from the area of Posavina, or Herzegovinians and Dalmations and others who came from other areas. And there were also wounded men, those who could not move. And we looked after them and tended to them, tried to dress their wounds with what we had. We tried to make do. And that is what I'm saying. I cannot simply -- it is almost beyond me how one goes through such conditions and yet survives. Later on when the Red Cross came, that is when we started getting medicines and that was a completely different situation then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get any medical supplies through Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard that something did come. But I did not talk with anyone in Merhamet. I do not know if they brought anything in or distributed. I did not communicate with them. I must admit that I did not have a personal contact with them. Perhaps somebody did. Perhaps Merhamet did bring in some medicines. I do not know if they did. But I'm not sure that I had all that many medicines to bring them. But I never communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they didn't -- they didn't communicate with you directly, as the doctor.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you -- the first time that you operated the clinic and people waited to see you, did anything happen to them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: In the early days, yes. In June. June was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to people who were waiting to see you, the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: We'd come in front of them together in that position, as I told you, and we'd get into the infirmary. They'd tell us to go to the infirmary. And we'd change. We had our white coats. And then they'd call them out. And once they were outside, they would be beaten often. For instance, they would reach the door all right on their own -- under their own power, under their own steam. And when they come in, you can't even recognise them. Right in front of the -- of the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have to issue death certificates?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who -- which -- I'm sorry, the person for whom you first had to issue a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a policeman before the war, and later on when he came to Manjaca I examined him one day. And it was a nice sunny day, about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon, because we, the doctors and nurses, were always there at the reception when new men arrived. So we would examine them in the infirmary and describe what they had -- what injuries they had perhaps got elsewhere. And this man -- and his name was Emir Mulalic, short. I know him because he was ill before the war and I sent him to the military hospital in Zagreb. So I examined him, and he had absolutely no injury, no visible injuries, nothing. So what we noted down was "no bruises, no injuries, nothing." The next day, between 12.00 and 13.00, there were very -- there was very loud shouts and they called to me because I was in the stable. I was called out to go there straight away. And I went there, and they told me that I had to go in and examine. And I went in and I saw on the table, I saw a guy who was dead. And they told me that he had fallen, that he was interrogated before that -- in the room where the investigators were, and that he had fallen and that that was how it happened. I examined him on the table. I took off his clothes. I looked him over. And his whole -- his chest -- the sternum, this was broken, and he was bleeding at the mouth and at the nose. But all this here was broken. And I took a notebook and I saw that the day before, he had been examined and that he had no injuries. But that is how this man ended. We established that, that he was dead. And after that, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic summoned me, Derviskadic, and we had to go to the administrative building, or, that is, to the office. A typewriter, a white table cloth, a table, and this is what he says to me. "Doctor, you must write a record of death and cause of death." And I had already done it before because I was the coroner for the Sanski Most and Prijedor areas before the war. And he says, "Well, write if you like that he died of pneumonia or a heart attack." And I said, "Lieutenant colonel, sir, how can I do it?" And he said, "Just as you did in school, when you had to describe how somebody had died of a heart attack, of pneumonia, that is what you should write." Well -- and I was thinking this was dead anyway, and I know what is in store for me if I don't do it. So I take it type -- type there on the table. I do not say what I saw. Really I said there was the discolourations on the body. I said myocardial infarction. And that was it. I signed it first and then the lieutenant colonel and after him Meho Derviskadic. The other one was Omer Filipovic and there were others, but they do not always all stick in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about Omer Filipovic in a minute. But I just want to ask you about this. You said you knew what would happen if you hadn't signed a false certificate, in other words, saying the man had died of pneumonia when he'd been -- his chest had been crushed or whatever. What did you think would happen?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Not the lungs but the chest, the sternum. Sternum. Well, I would have paid a very high price, perished. You can't disobey. That was fascism, and there's no discussing -- I mean, I said it before. I'm saying now before these gentlemen. This is a well oiled fascism. That is the situation. When you try to annihilate the whole people. And it was -- you really had to apply all your wits to survive somehow, to make it through somehow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Mr. Mulalic. I'll deal with Mr. Filipovic in a moment. But do you remember a man from Kljuc dying?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I say I do remember that man from Kljuc. There was first a young man, a well-built, strong young man. But he was all covered in bruises too. And he was taken away. A car came and took him to Banja Luka, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That is where he was buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to sign a death certificate for him as well?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't ask me to do it for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Omer Filipovic, what did you know or what did you see of what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I told you already. By then I already had to also somehow manage the trauma that I had suffered. Now, nobody hit me, nobody beat me, but I had suffered a mental trauma. Every time I went to examine, they threatened me. So that I have to look after my mental health. So on one occasion, I was standing next to a small group but there were two policemen. And Omer Filipovic, who was at the headmaster in a secondary school and taught philosophy -- and there was a conversation. I was a few metres away, 5, 6 metres away. And I heard this conversation, how hard it is on people, and Omer saying, and Omer was saying how he would write down his memoirs and once he left the camp how he would write his memoirs and say how he had fared in Manjaca. And at that moment a policeman cursed -- use a dirty word and said, "Omer, you'll never write that." And then the attitude towards Omer changed. They started beating him, persecuting him, physically and psychologically, and before he left he was taken to the solitary confinement several times and was lying next to me in the stable, and nobody dared to go. He was like at the end of this room here and I was like this. And nobody dared approach him, go to him, give him water or anything. And when he was taken away from there one night, the next day around 10.00 I was called out and this other doctor and we went down. The door was open for us. And in front of that was the hearse and a driver already arrived from Banja Luka, and inside -- and it's a narrow room. A metre and a half or something. Omer was lying on his back, dead, bloody. There was a fire extinguisher next to him, you know, like this one, and its bottom was bloody. Omer was -- had been killed. We wrapped him in a blanket, put him in a coffin. And then the ambulance car arrived. And that is what I know about Omer Filipovic. What he did before and how he behaved before, I know nothing about that. But this is what I know about his death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Two things. First of all, you've told us that one night at 10.00 -- sorry, the next day -- no. I'll start this again. He was taken away from the stable in which you were one night.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: He couldn't walk. He was carried out. He could not walk. He was carried away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you told us you were called out the next day. And where was he when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But where?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That evening. That evening. Before he went to the stable. And then from the stable he was carried to the isolation cell, and that is where he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is that where you say you saw his body and the fire extinguisher?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct any sort of post-mortem examination of him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't need any post-mortem. One could establish death and all the certain and uncertain causes of death. The man was liquidated. He was killed. It was a violent death. He was covered in blood around his mouth and nose. The fire extinguisher next to him was also bloodstained in the area where he was hit, and that was around his chest. And that is how we were given a blanket to wrap him in and carry him out. And the driver, who was a very -- who treated us very decently and gave us a packet of cigarettes each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you made to -- were you made to write a death certificate for him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, I don't remember. I did write several death certificates. I believe his was one of them. But I did several of them. But that was seven months, and there were several dead people and only one from Teslic was the only one who died of natural causes. All the others died violent deaths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we -- I'll come back to the numbers in a moment. Do you remember Esad Bender?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Bender. E-R. He was allegedly from what I heard there, he was a poor man and he was a journeyman and used to work for Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in the same stable as you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the middle row.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how shall I tell you what happened to him? The same as to the all the others. He was taken out, beaten, beaten every night. No sooner does night fall, they come and beat, and you have to listen to this and you must be very stable mentally to survive, to avoid being traumatised. As soon as the night comes. So this Bender was taken out several times and beaten. And one morning, after 10.00 or 11.00 I was lying there in the first row and he was lying in the middle row and they called me there and I looked and the man was dead. And they said that he was suffering from cancer that, he had a carcinoma. But nobody knew whether he did have a carcinoma or anything. Those were bruises. Those were injuries. That is a violent death. I did that and I was an expert witness in the district court in Banja Luka before the war. I did the post-mortems. I did exhumations. And it was clear as daylight to me. And every word I'm saying here is gospel truth. He died a violent death, but also the record was taken and I was told that he was suffering from a carcinoma. And that is what I wrote down, because there was no alternative. That is how it was. It is horrible -- I mean, it was horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that only one man that you can remember died of natural causes, and that was a man from Teslic. Over the period that you were in Manjaca, between June and November, roughly --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: From Teslic. There's a location called Teslic. There's a rehabilitation centre there called Teslic. And from this town of Teslic there was an elderly man who brought with him his medical documents when he was arrested, and it said in those documents that he had carcinoma of the lungs and he died of natural causes. Nobody beat him. He died. And his body was driven away. What happened after, I don't know. That is the only case of natural death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly in that period, between June and November, how many people do you think died in Manjaca from beatings or other killings?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not such a large number if we were to judge by the number. I think 10 to 15 men, not more. I'm not sure. Things may have happened that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beatings. In your own stable, you say the number varied. But how would the beatings take place? Would they take place in the stable or outside?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, either they were beaten up and they died or they would be taken away and they would never come back. And we didn't know what happened to him. Or he would be exchanged, or there were cases of people of 60 and who were sick, to be released, so that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You misunderstand. I plan to come on to --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Numbers changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If -- there were beatings, you've told us. Would the beatings take place inside the table or outside the stable?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Inside the stables but in particular -- particularly outside during the night. As night fell, they would come and call men out. There was a judge who was called out two or three times. And luckily he did not respond. He certainly would not have lived to see the day. And they would take people out by calling their surnames. And the man either didn't come back or he would come back beaten up. And this happened mostly at night, after 11.00 or 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the minefield that was put down. Was anybody ever injured by a mine?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A young man from Kotor Varos. He was washing his shirt and jacket, and he was about to hang it on the fence and the mines were laid - and we all were aware of that. Unfortunately he stepped on it. And I was standing there. It was right next to my stable. I was standing there when I heard the explosion. He had big rubber boots on, and the boot went 20 metres into the air. We ran up to him, took him to the surgery, put a compress. His right leg had been cut off below the knee, and his left also -- the lower leg had been destroyed. We did what we could. An ambulance came and took him off to Banja Luka to the surgery ward. What happened, I don't know. I never heard anything about it after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about interrogations? Were you yourself questioned or interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I was the first to be interrogated when I arrived at Manjaca, the first. And he was correct with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: He asked me how I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all -- I'm sorry. Where were you taken to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: A policeman came to the stable and took me to the command, into a room there. I sat down. They gave me a piece of paper and said, "Write whatever you have to say about yourself." I didn't write a lot. And then he put questions to me. Had I done my military service, did I have arms, had I been on the front, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: We had a good --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. Sorry. You wanted to say -- you had a good ...?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: We finished it around 2.00 a.m. It started in the evening, and we finished about 2.00 a.m., this conversation. He told me his name was Vanja, that he was a lawyer. He was short. And afterwards he helped me quite a bit compared to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be walking around here if it hadn't been for him in Manjaca. Just the same applies to the commander in Sanski Most that I mentioned, regardless of everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This lawyer, Vanja, was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a camouflage uniform, you know, the one that is fashionable nowadays in armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you of any allegations that had been made against you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that there were accusations, that I was one of those people who was fighting against the Serb people, et cetera. That was the policies. It was a political act, which was common knowledge. All this came from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm interested in -- not common knowledge but what he actually said to you. Can you remember now what he said you were being accused of?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that I was accused of being on the front line, fighting, that before that I was in the SDA party and I was -- I'm still in that party. I'm not hiding that fact, I'm still in the party, but I don't wish to have any positions. I'm just a member of the municipal board in Sanski Most. Because of my profession and my work, I have abandoned any political functions. The fact that I was a Muslim, a member of the SDA party, the Party of Democratic Action and so on. That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Serbian democratic party and nothing happened to him. But this was all part of the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any reference to any medical mall practice that you were supposed to have engaged in?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Yes. A thing -- one forgets things. It was ten years ago. I didn't study for this. When I was studying for my baccalaureate, I would take notes. But I didn't prepare myself for this. But yes. Allegedly I had given injections to Serb children that I shouldn't have given, and I was a specialist of internal medicine. I can't remember when I last examined a child. Apparently I had given them injections in Lusci Palanka, also injections to women for them not to get pregnant and -- so that Serb children would not be born. But I said, "Sir, Mr. Investigator, who would discover such an injection in the world today, he would win the Nobel Prize. When you think of the Pope and all these campaigns nowadays. You see, I have to speak out sometimes. We have to understand. There's not much we have to discuss here, you see. These are facts. It was fascism. It was to destroy two peoples. And there's no dilemma about that. A doctor, Filipovic, he was a gynaecologist - he's an American now - he came beaten up. Derviskadic examined him. He didn't know what to do. And then he asked me, "Should I go to Banja Luka to the hospital?" And I said, "don't go. We'll help you." He went to Banja Luka and came back. And he got it on his head. And that is the truth. He was also charged of giving injections to Serb women. My wife is Serbian. I could have given her an injection, and then I wouldn't have to take her to a gynaecologists for examinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was anything finally said to you during this interrogation or later about what was going to happen to you? Were you going to be brought before a court?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that these political representatives who advocated such a position, the position of the Crisis Staff of Bosnian Krajina and the Serb republic -- it is the same theology -- no, sorry, ideology. The same way of thinking. It is clear that they would be liquidated, that only those -- that those who were not guilty would be sent home. But it would be best to go to third countries. I too was told when people saw for themselves that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry, doctor. I know it's difficult and emotional, but all I want to know is were you told --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I won't do it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I want to know is were you told whether or not you'd been brought -- you would be brought before a court.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you told would happen to you when you'd be brought before the court?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what happens when you go before a military tribunal, especially under such charges. That I am a nationalist, et cetera. And I don't see any such nationalism. And when I look around here and elsewhere, there were the smallest -- among Muslims, they were the fewest who fanned ethnic hatred. There's no such thing here in The Hague or elsewhere. So we know exactly who did what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you didn't -- you couldn't complain about the way you were treated by this lawyer during your interrogation. What about other people who were taken for interrogation? Did anything happen to them?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Each one of them came back beaten. I told you. One had to be strong to preserve one's mental health. They would invite me to have whiskey with them, to get me drunk so that under the influence of alcohol I might have said something. I don't hate anyone. I'm related to Serbs. But when the commander fell ill, the warden fell ill, and then I treat them and then they have to go to the clinic and then peasants would come to the surgery for examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, let's deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would invite you to exercise a little bit of control over the witness; otherwise I will do it. He's your witness. I wouldn't like to interfere much. But I think he's getting a little bit too excited about the whole affair and he's running --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to answer the question -- try to answer the question and just the question, sir, because otherwise you've been making the Prosecutor's life difficult in a way. I mean, it's -- I do appreciate that you have problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have problems. I just -- it's just -- it's just difficult to stop him. But I'm doing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try and -- I do appreciate that -- I think he has to draw a line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- I think, yes. I understand what Your Honour means, and I'll try and keep it a bit shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not your fault. It's his fault; not yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that they would invite you to have whiskey with them. Who do you mean? The guards?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The police commander and a lieutenant and other members of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us in that same answer that when the commander fell ill and the warden fell ill, you treated them. So you treated Popovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Popovic and another policeman called Spaga -- nicknamed Spaga. He got a high fever. I tried with infusion solution and everything else. It didn't work. And I sent him to the clinic for infectious diseases. He spent a month there and he returned. The man changed his opinion about me altogether and everything else. And the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, had angina pectoris. He had heart problems. I would send him to his colleagues I used to work with in Banja Luka, Dr. Ristic and I forget now all the names and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to turn not last 15 minutes or so to a slightly different topic. The water at the camp -- I'd like you to have a look, please, at a couple of documents, which are, first of all, P398. That's in the Banja Luka binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 27th of July from the 1st Krajina Corps. And it deals with results of tests of water for the -- I can never pronounce that word -- Karadordevo farm and the prisoner of war camp in Manjaca. And it talks about repairing the water pipes. Now, first of all, what was the water like at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in the stable at first there was an old water tap that you could use. But it stopped working about ten -- after ten days, and there was no water after that. But detainees would go to the lake in line and bring water. And sometimes you would even see tadpoles in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the quality of the water like, then?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Dreadful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is an order of some kind to repair water pipes, saying prisoners -- there are enough prisoners of war who can be engaged as labourers with the appropriate security. Was there any such repair of the water pipes?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw any repairs being done, nor were any repairs done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because if we look at the next document that -- just very quickly, which is P406, please. That's an order dated -- I'm sorry, it's a request for urgent intervention due to failure to respond, 5th of August, 1992, where they repeat that request for solution to the problem of water. There was no reaction after that, no repair of the water pipes after that either, doctor? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, nothing was ever repaired -- nothing was repaired, nor was there any water afterwards. There was at the beginning for a few days, and then it stopped. No repairs were done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about labour? Were prisoners made to work?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want you to look at another series of documents, please. First of all, P417, a document dated the 22nd of August, 1992. And it's headed "Reconstruction works on the church in the village of Sljivno, order." And then it's -- and the order comes on behalf of General Talic. It says: "On the basis of demonstrated need to repair the Serbian Orthodox church in the village of Sljivno and in order to ensure the work is done and material used according to plan," he then issued instructions, which at item 5 said that "The collection centre at Manjaca shall provide the work force to carry out all the work on the site, and the head of the centre shall personally answer to me for this." Do you remember prisoners having to work on reconstructing a church?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Not reconstruction. The construction of a church, which was roughly 12 by 10 metres, a beautifully built church, as said in the order, and it was done by the detainees. You had all the crafts represented, from electricians to assembly workers. Up to 1.000 men would work on it a day, on the church, and the church was built.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look now, please, at document numbered P429 and P428. We might as well have the two together. In P429 -- well, just -- sorry, P428. The 1st of October there's a request for the engagements of prisoners of war from Manjaca prisoner of war camp for works to be carried out by the 1st Pontoon Battalion, loading and reloading wood, 20 prisoners of war for a period of ten days. "The battalion can provide its own security and accommodation for prisoners, the prison building in Troselji near Nova Topola." Do you remember any prisoners being sent off to an area near Nova Topola?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I can't really remember. But they went wherever they were called. Probably they went there too, because they went to cut wood. A Catholic was killed cutting wood, in fact, at Manjaca. I just remembered that. That's the truth. This is the truth. Yes, yes. They went to Jajce and all over the place, to the hydro power station and other works that they had to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then the other document is a request for Manjaca prisoners for road construction, camouflage company, and fortification company. To your knowledge, were prisoners taken to work in areas where there was fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't say. They didn't dig. There was no fighting. In Banja Luka there was no war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well, it may -- if we look at the next two documents -- the last two documents on this, please, P424 and P436. 424 is an order dated the 22nd of September -- sorry. I've got it slightly out of order -- asking, also authorising, signed by Colonel Vukelic, that prisoners from Manjaca should work on a farm in Banja Luka, up to 60 prisoners of war daily. Do you remember prisoners being taken to work on a farm near Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. People were taken for agricultural work. Only I'd be wrong if I say I know of this particular farm, but I know that they were taken to do farm work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally this, P436, dated the 5th of November. This is taking people from Manjaca to clean up Jajce hydro electric powerplants and engage them until the powerplants become operative, and then a military battalion to secure the prisoners. "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic shall answer to me for engaging the prisoners of war, and Colonel Vukelic shall answer to me for the entire operation of cleaning up the Jajce 1 hydro electric plants." And there's a -- it appears to be signed on behalf of Talic. Do you remember prisoners having to go to this particular hydro electric plant in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The hydro electric plant in Jajce, 1 and 2. They did go there and work there, especially people who had those crafts, to get the powerplant going again. They did go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Your Honour, that completes that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. We'll continue tomorrow morning -- tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. Hopefully we will finish tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be nice. If possible. I have a lot of business and professional obligations to attend to in my hospital. But I am ready to stay for as long as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doctor, we'll do our utmost to keep you here the least possible. And I'm sure that everyone will cooperate and understand that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of June, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
